implementation_notes: pika turns the broker into the store with three calls: channel.confirm_delivery() enables publisher confirms, basic_publish(..., properties=pika.BasicProperties(delivery_mode=2, message_id=order_id)) marks the message persistent, and the call then blocks until the broker confirms (RabbitMQ confirms a persistent message to a durable - best quorum - queue only after it is persisted). On the consuming side, basic_consume plus basic_ack after the business commit is the receiver half, with prefetch_count bounding in-flight unacknowledged messages. The classic channel/consumer objects are still the right shape here; Python offers no simpler durable-messaging idiom beyond a database outbox (next variant).
code_sketch:
ch.confirm_delivery()                                   # publisher confirms on
ch.queue_declare("orders", durable=True,
                 arguments={"x-queue-type": "quorum"})  # replicated store
ch.basic_publish(exchange="", routing_key="orders", body=body,
                 properties=pika.BasicProperties(delivery_mode=2, message_id=order_id),
                 mandatory=True)                            # raises on nack/unroutable

def on_message(ch, method, props, body):
    save_order(body)                              # business commit
    ch.basic_ack(method.delivery_tag)              # then the delivery ack
pitfalls: confirm_delivery() only affects publishes issued on that channel afterwards and raises UnroutableError/NackError instead of returning a flag - catching and continuing loses messages.
delivery_mode=2 does nothing useful on a transient queue or an auto-delete exchange; the queue's durability is the other half of the configuration.

pika channels are not thread-safe and the blocking adapter must not run long work inside a consumer callback (heartbeats and the ack window break) - hand work to a worker thread with add_callback_threadsafe.
basic_ack before the database commit converts a crash into silent loss, and acking twice closes the channel with a PRECONDITION_FAILED error.

variants.name: Transactional outbox table with a polling dispatcher
variants.idiom_name: outbox row in the business transaction + FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED poller
variants.implementation_notes: With the business state in the same database, the outbox replaces the messaging store: add the message row inside the business transaction (one session.commit() writes state and message), and let a dispatcher send and delete it - SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on Postgres, or a single-writer BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction on SQLite. The database's WAL is the durable copy and 'write plus send' becomes one atomic commit, so no XA and no dual-write window is needed. This is the idiomatic Python shape when Redis/RabbitMQ cannot join the transaction; use a broker client variant when the throughput per message matters more than atomicity.
variants.code_sketch:
with Session(engine) as s, s.begin():            # one transaction
    s.add(Order(id=oid, status="new"))
    s.add(Outbox(id=oid, topic="orders", payload=body))   # durable with the state

row = s.execute(text("SELECT id, topic, payload FROM outbox "
                     "ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1")).one()
broker.send(row.topic, row.payload)              # at-least-once
s.execute(text("DELETE FROM outbox WHERE id=:i"), {"i": row.id})
s.commit()                                        # forget only after the send
pitfalls: Calling the broker outside the transaction that wrote the row reintroduces the dual write; the dispatcher must not start before the transaction commits (enqueue after commit hooks are safer than a nested session).
Sending and deleting in separate transactions duplicates on a crash - intended at-least-once, so the consumer needs dedup or idempotence on the outbox id.
SQLite needs WAL mode and BEGIN IMMEDIATE (or a single writer) because it has no SKIP LOCKED; concurrent pollers otherwise raise 'database is locked'.
An outbox without retention or archive cleans up turns into an ever-growing table, and a poller that stops logging is an invisible delivery outage.
